site.title: — Münster AR
index.title:
A gargoyle
rarely comes alone
index.description-before: Whether they're animals, people, or monsters, discover more than
index.text: You can get to know 13 of them on an augmented reality tour.
index.swipe: Swipe left to proceed to the next step.
index.manual-first-step-text: Find a suitable wall at the cathedral and point your camera at it.
index.manual-first-step-alt: A camera is pointed at a section of the cathedral's wall
index.manual-second-step-text: Scan the wall surface until the 3D model appears.
index.manual-second-step-alt: A 3D model of a gargoyle appears on the wall
index.manual-third-step-text: Tap the info button to learn more about the gargoyle.
index.manual-third-step-alt: The Info button in the user interface becomes tappable
index.first-tip: Look for symbols, inscriptions, or conspicuous areas of rock.
index.second-tip: The 3D models are always hidden on flat walls, not in corners or along edges.
index.third-tip: From the scanning position, you can spot the stone gargoyle above you.
index.fourth-tip: In bright sunlight or heavy rain, detection may be impaired under certain circumstances.
index.fifth-tip: To help you find your way around, just take a look at the map — it shows you where the gargoyle models are hidden.
index.notice-text: Due to construction or events on Münsterplatz, some hiding spots may be temporarily inaccessible. Just visit these gargoyles at a later time.
index.camera-access-text: The AR app requires access to your camera. When you launch it, your browser will ask for your permission. Allow camera access so that the app can work.
app.title: Hunt the gargoyles
app.info.title.15: Man in a hood, holding a flagon
app.info.none: Please scan a gargoyle to get information about it.
app.info.0: Plaster cast of a 13th-century gargoyle from the Freiburger Minster. A man carries a unicorn on his back with its legs over his shoulders. The unicorn's ears and the man's nose were already missing from the stone, when it was cast. The original can still be found at the cathedral.
app.info.1: Because of the open book he holds, this gargoyle from 1913 is also called “the scholar”. The water was emitted from above the brim of his hat. He replaced a partially lost predecessor that dated back to 19th century. 2005 “the scholar”, in turn, had to be removed from the cathedral for safety. It remains unknown whether this version of the gargoyle is a hidden portrait of an actual person.
app.info.2: This scrawny little dog stalks through the scrub at the side portal of the cathedral. That is why its back is connected to the wall behind it and it is smaller than many other gargoyles of the cathedral.
app.info.3: This gargoyle is one of two running horses who mirror each other. It has lost part of its legs, ears and muzzle due to weathering. When a copy was crafted, the muzzle was reconstructed with modelling material. The partner to this gargoyle remains at the cathedral of Freiburg im Breisgau to this day.
app.info.4: This gargoyle is composed of features from various creatures. While the big head with the partly missing muzzle resembles a dog with floppy ears, the clawed feet look almost bird-like. Behind one front leg hides a bird of prey next to some foliage. Until it was removed from the cathedral in 1998, this gargoyle shared its spot with part of its predecessor. When most of the predecessor was lost to an undocumented event, a new gargolye was installed above it - instead of removing the old one completely from the wall.
app.info.5: This beast combines the traits of several animals. The head could be that of a dog, the tight curls, the round ears and the long tail with a tassel more likely belong to a lion and the feathers on its neck and shoulders as well as the claws on its forelegs hint towards a bird. It is one of many examples at the Freiburger Minster of the creative work of medieval stonemasons. The reddish color of one of its front legs indicates that it was repaired at a later date, probably during the 20th century.
app.info.6: At first glance, this gargoyle appears to be a dog. The body is gaunt, ribs clearly visible, skin wrinkled on its hind legs, resembling a greyhound. In contrast the neck seems too thick and the head too large and massive, but still similar to a dog with ears that are laid back. One detail does not fit though: the two cloven hooves on its forelegs clearly mark this beast as something different. As monstrous.
app.info.7: The tangled limbs of this man are the reason why this gargoyle is also referred to as the acrobat. He has a large and prominent goiter on his throat, a medical condition widely associated with iodine deficiency. The gargoyle's arms were lost at some unknown point in time. However on his hands and the stubs of his arms remain signs of an effort to reattach the arms after they had broken off.
app.info.8: This crouching skeleton with a scroll between its legs and a snake curled to its side lost most of its thin limbs – both arms, a part of its left leg and its head – due to weathering. The head with an almost abstract looking, bulky face is a later addition, held in place by two clamps on either side of its neck. When the gargoyle was replaced in 1939, the head was changed to a horned skull, adopting only the curly hair from the predecessor.
app.info.9: A lean male hound towers proudly over the captured hare that lays beneath its paws. This sculpture is one of the many gargoyles of the Freiburger Minster. Even though the underside is greatly affected by weathering and the muzzle is almost entirely lost, there are still many astonishing details left, for example the fine lines defining the dog's eyes.
app.info.10: A griffin is a mythical creature that is part eagle and part lion. Only the head and wings of this gargoyle are those of an eagle, although it has teeth in its beak. The body and ears belong to a lion. In its paws it presents the coat of arms of the Blumeneck family, the donors of the chapel on whose exterior the gargoyle is placed.
app.info.11: This fish-like beast with its coiled, scaley body resembles the depiction of a dolphin from the Baroque era. It was created 1781 by Joseph Hörr and thus is the only original gargoyle whose stonemason is known by name. Over time, cracks formed throughout the stone. They were temporarily secured with wire and a metal band, but ultimately the gargoyle was replaced by a copy in 1987.
app.info.12: This gargoyle sits on the wall of the Mount Olivet-Chapel of the Freiburger Minster, one claw scratching the chin below the maw with jagged teeth, the other claw holding a scroll. Though part of the scroll is lost, the remaining piece reads “A […] DOMINI” and therefor refers to the year of its creation.
app.info.13: On first glance this gargoyle appears to be a big heap of wavy wool, as many distinctive elements have been impaired by weathering. The head broke roughly in half, leaving only the eyes and the base of the nose intact. Behind the rim of locks that divides the face from the wool clad body are remnants of the curved horns. They reach towards the small tips of the ears. The left front leg is streched forward as if to scratch behind one ear. In 2003 the gargoyle was replaced with a copy for which all those details were carefully reconstructed.
app.info.14: This gargoyle shows a man carrying a billy goat and it is one of few gargoyles, where one figure carries the other. In this case though, it seems to be quite forceful and one-sided: The man grabs the billy goat by its goatee with one hand, the other probably held onto a horn. In contrast the billy goat has its legs folded beneath its belly and doesn’t hold onto the man at all. Parts of the ensemble, such as the billy goat's horns or the face and one hand of the man are missing. This led to a replacement of the gargoyle by a copy in 2005.
app.info.15: High up on the tower of the Freiburger Minster there is a group of seven sculptures which look like gargoyles, they however do not have a gutter through which water can be drained away. The man with a flagon is a later addition to the group and replaced an unknown predecessor, possibly lost to damage caused by lightning. While the rest of the group each represent one of the seven cardinal sins, this man cannot be ascribed to one. It is plausible that the theme of the vices was not revisited when this sculpture was created in the 16th century. While the original still remains at its intended place, this model originates from a plaster cast, made in 1914 as documentation.
app.info.16: High up on the tower of the Freiburger Minster there is a group of seven sculptures which look like gargoyles, they however do not have a gutter through which water can be drained away. The originals, dating from around 1320, represented the seven cardinal sins. In this case, “Pride” is depicted as a knight in full armor and a tunic. The original was replaced by a copy in 1915. A year prior a plaster cast was made as documentation. The model is based on this cast.
app.info.17: High up on the tower of the Freiburger Minster there is a group of seven sculptures which look like gargoyles, they however do not have a gutter through which water can be drained away. The originals, dating from around 1320, represented the seven cardinal sins. In this case, “Gluttony” is depicted as a boar. The original was replaced by a copy in 1915. A year prior a plaster cast was made as documentation. The model is based on this cast.
